messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mele was a 57-year-old architect who came to treatment nearly a year after her younger sister died following a sudden medical crisis. She had been with her in the hospital through the last chaotic hours, standing in a fluorescent corridor outside the intensive care unit while staff moved quickly around her and voices overlapped in clipped medical language she could not follow. What stayed with her was not a single image so much as a whole sensory field: the sharp antiseptic smell on her hands and clothes, the disorienting wash of incomprehensible chatter at the nurses’ station, and the layout of the hospital itself—the long hallway, the waiting room alcove, the turn toward the elevators. She had gone in believing that if she stayed close and listened carefully she would understand what was happening. Instead she experienced the night as bewildering and final, and afterward those specific cues became charged in a way that felt immediate and bodily.

In the months that followed, those reminders appeared where she did not expect them. On building site visits she found herself freezing in institutional-looking corridors that echoed the hospital’s geometry. If she passed a clinic lobby or caught the smell of disinfectant in an office restroom, her chest tightened and her mind snapped back to the night her sister died. Even overheard conversations in languages she did not understand, or several people talking at once in a way she could not parse, could make her feel abruptly untethered. In those moments she did not just remember the loss; she was seized by the old conviction that life could turn incomprehensible without warning, that no one was really looking after anyone, and that whatever trust she once had—in people, in order, in any larger sense that things happened for a reason—had drained away. The reminders seemed to prove what she had come to believe: that the world was indifferent and that nothing in her life carried the meaning it used to. Once that belief had taken hold, she moved through ordinary places as if they were full of hidden confirmations. A hallway she would once have barely noticed, a sharp chemical smell, or a burst of overlapping conversation now caught and held her attention precisely because she had come to expect that any confusing sensory detail might be the start of another moment of helplessness.

Those beliefs began to shape how she moved through her days. Mele stopped meeting friends for dinner and gradually ignored messages she would once have answered right away. She said it was easier not to have to sit across from people who might look at her too closely. She had come to feel that the loss was somehow visible on her, as if others could detect what had happened just by seeing her face and posture, and she dreaded the exposure of ordinary social contact. She also became rigid about avoiding hospitals, ambulances, and even routine physical examinations. She knew this created practical problems—she postponed her own medical care and rerouted herself through the city to avoid passing the medical center near her firm—but it felt safer than risking the flood of sensations and the collapse in meaning that followed. At the same time, she pushed herself into punishing exercise, sometimes running for far longer than her knees could tolerate, because exhaustion gave her a narrow, controllable focus that blotted out thought for a while.

These strategies, however, tightened the very world she was trying to manage. The less she saw friends, the more convinced she became that she was fundamentally cut off from other people and from the person she had been before her sister’s death. Long solitary runs left her physically depleted and emotionally flat, reinforcing her sense that nothing genuinely nourished her anymore. Avoiding medical settings spared her immediate distress, but it also made hospitals seem more forbidden and dangerous with each passing week. By shrinking her life around what she could not face, she found herself reading the shrinkage as evidence that life itself had lost meaning.

Her work as an architect gave these patterns a daily foothold. She had once loved walking through unfinished buildings and imagining the life that would fill them. Now certain spaces felt treacherous. A client meeting in a new health-care development was especially difficult; the clean synthetic smell of the interior and the long, bright corridor outside the conference room hit her before she could prepare. She left abruptly, told a colleague she felt unwell, and later insisted he cover future meetings at medical sites. Afterward she was ashamed and more certain that people could see something damaged in her. Since then she has become hyperaware in many public interiors, scanning for the smell of antiseptic, listening for speech she cannot make sense of, noticing spatial arrangements that resemble that hospital floor. The more she avoids, the more quickly those cues seem to find her.

By the time Mele sought help, her world had narrowed to work, home, and exercise. Her friends had largely stopped asking her out. She had delayed a needed physical for months. What finally brought her in was a moment at a project presentation when overlapping side conversations in the room made her lose her place entirely; she felt exposed, hollow, and suddenly certain that there was no point to anything she was building. What frightened her most was the sense that this was becoming permanent—that she would go on arranging her life around corridors, smells, and voices, cut off from people and from any belief that life could hold meaning again.
